args.text: ### Project Directory Setup First up, you'll knock together a directory to keep yer Rust code in. Rust couldn't give a toss where yer code lives, but for the exercises and projects in this book, we reckon you make a _projects_ directory in yer home directory and keep all yer projects in there. Nice and tidy. Fire up a terminal and punch in these commands to make a _projects_ directory, and a directory for the "Hello, world!" project inside the _projects_ directory. For Linux, macOS, and PowerShell on Windows, bung in this: ```console $ mkdir ~/projects $ cd ~/projects $ mkdir hello_world $ cd hello_world ``` For Windows CMD, it's this one: ```cmd > mkdir "%USERPROFILE%\projects" > cd /d "%USERPROFILE%\projects" > mkdir hello_world > cd hello_world ``` ### Rust Program Basics Next, whip up a brand-spankin'-new source file and call it _main.rs_. Rust files always finish with the _.rs_ extension. If ya want more than one word in yer filename, the done thing is to stick an underscore between 'em. So it's _hello_world.rs_, not _helloworld.rs_, which just looks like someone's leanin' on the keyboard. Now open up that _main.rs_ file ya just made and type in the code in Listing 1-1. ```rust fn main() { println!("Hello, world!"); } ``` Save the file and duck back to yer terminal window in the _~/projects/hello_world_ directory. On Linux or macOS, punch in these commands to compile the file and give it a run: ```console $ rustc main.rs $ ./main Hello, world! ``` On Windows, ya type the command `.\main` instead of `./main`: ```powershell > rustc main.rs > .\main Hello, world! ``` Doesn't matter what operatin' system you're on, the string `Hello, world!` should pop up in the terminal. If it doesn't show, have a squiz back at the [“Troubleshooting”][troubleshooting] bit of the Installation section for ways to get yerself some help. If `Hello, world!` did print, good on ya! You've officially written a Rust program. That makes ya a Rust programmer. Welcome aboard, mate, kettle's on.
